docs.title: AMS Digital Scholar
docs.text: Welcome to the AMS Digital Scholar (DS) resource hub. This site is dedicated to the training and development of AMS staff in the field of digital scholarship.

docs.title: Our Mission
docs.text: To bridge the gap between traditional archaeological research and modern digital workflows, ensuring AMS remains at the forefront of the consultancy sector.

docs.title: Current Focus
docs.text:
• Reference Management: Implementing Zotero for robust citation and research organisation.
  • Knowledge Graphs: Exploring Obsidian and other networked-thought tools.
  • Automated Synthesis: Integrating RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) with academic libraries.

docs.title: Getting Started: The Learning Pathway
docs.text:
To begin your journey as an AMS Digital Scholar, we recommend following our Research Pathways, which guide you from initial discovery to final synthesis:

  1. Our Strategy: Understand the "Research Chain" and the Consultant-Scholar model.
  2. Phase 1: Discovery: Map the research landscape using Perplexity and Research Rabbit.
  3. Phase 2: Collection: Build your digital library with Zotero and Tropy.
  4. Phase 3: Annotation: Peer-review and annotate evidence via Hypothesis.
  5. Phase 4: Synthesis: Generate grounded insights with NotebookLM and Obsidian.

For a complete list of step-by-step instructions, visit the Tutorials Archive.

docs.title: The AMS Digital Scholar: Discovery-to-Delivery Workflow
docs.text: This guide outlines the overarching vision for the AMS Digital Scholar (DS) ecosystem. It defines how our suite of tools operates as a unified "research chain," transforming raw archaeological data and obscure grey literature into high-fidelity, professional consultancy reports.

docs.title: 1. The Vision: The "Consultant-Scholar" Model
docs.text: At AMS, we do not view research and consultancy as separate silos. The Digital Scholar programme empowers our staff to act as Consultant-Scholars—professionals who use academic-grade digital tools to provide commercial clients with superior site interpretations, robust risk assessments, and citable archaeological narratives.

docs.title: 2. The DS Research Chain
docs.text:
The ecosystem is envisaged as a continuous pipeline where each tool serves a specific, high-value function.

Phase Core Tools Primary Function AMS Advantage 1. Discovery Perplexity, ResearchRabbit Mapping the landscape of known data. Rapidly identify obscure TII reports and foundational academic papers. 2. Collection Zotero, Tropy Building the project-specific "Digital Library." Centralised, team-wide access to every source and site photo with rich metadata. 3. Annotation Hypothesis, Zotero Reader Deep reading and peer-review of evidence. Collaborative, real-time highlighting of planning conditions and site reports. 4. Synthesis NotebookLM, Obsidian Grounded AI reasoning and knowledge mapping. Zero-hallucination synthesis of dense EIARs and linking contexts to finds. 5. Production AMS Document Factory Final report generation and delivery. Automated compliance with AMS branding and linguistic standards.

docs.title: Discovery: The Intelligence Layer
docs.text:
• Perplexity: Unlike standard search, Perplexity provides cited summaries of regional archaeological contexts (e.g., "Mesolithic activity in Co. Clare").
  • ResearchRabbit: Visualises citation networks, ensuring we don't just find a paper, but also every subsequent study that has challenged or supported its findings.

docs.title: Collection: The Reference & Visual Archive
docs.text:
• Zotero: Serves as the company's "Memory." It manages the vast volume of grey literature that is often lost in standard file-server structures.
  • Tropy: Bridges the gap between raw field photography and the formal archive. It ensures that every photo of a find or section is described with Dublin Core metadata before it leaves the project team.

docs.title: Annotation: The Collaborative Layer
docs.text: • Hypothesis: Allows senior consultants to "live-review" a team member's research by annotating the source material directly on the web or in PDF format. This ensures that the evidence-base for a DBA or EIAR is rigorously peer-reviewed.

docs.title: Synthesis: The "Second Brain" & AI Engine
docs.text:
• Google NotebookLM: Provides a "Safe AI" environment. By grounding the AI strictly in our Zotero-managed PDFs, we can query thousands of pages of site data without the risk of fabricated information.
  • Obsidian: Acts as the long-term knowledge graph. It allows us to see connections between disparate sites (e.g., linking a specific pottery type in Co. Meath to a similar assemblage in Co. Kildare) that would otherwise remain hidden in separate folders.

docs.title: 4. Operational Guardrails: The CRAV Protocol
docs.text: To ensure the integrity of the Digital Scholar ecosystem, all outputs must pass through the Check, Review, Approve, Verify (CRAV) protocol: 1. Check: AI-generated summaries must be checked against the original sources. 2. Review: Peer-review of annotations in Hypothesis. 3. Approve: Management approval of the synthesis in Obsidian. 4. Verify: Final verification of links and citations before report production.

docs.title: 5. Summary of the Workflow
docs.text:
1. Search via ResearchRabbit/Perplexity to find the best evidence.
  2. Sync those sources to a Zotero Group Library.
  3. Annotate key findings collaboratively using Hypothesis.
  4. Synthesise the data in NotebookLM for rapid drafting.
  5. Build the final narrative in Obsidian for export to the AMS Document Engine.

By adopting this chain, AMS ensures that every report we produce is not just a document, but a verified asset in our growing digital knowledge ecosystem.

docs.title: AMS Digital Scholar: Research & Benchmarking
docs.text: The Digital Scholar (DS) research hub contains in-depth analysis, tool benchmarking, and strategic evaluations of digital scholarship applications.

docs.title: Current Research
docs.text:

This repository is maintained by the AI Strategy team as part of the AMS Digital Transformation.

docs.title: Digital Scholar: Future Programme Proposals
docs.text: This document outlines strategic initiatives and technical enhancements proposed for the expansion of the AMS Digital Scholar (DS) programme. These items are for management consideration to drive deeper adoption and professional excellence across the consultancy.

docs.title: 1. DS 'Lunch & Learn' Tactical Series
docs.text: A series of 15-minute, high-impact briefings recorded for the DS site, focusing on specific "Technical Wins": * Photo Efficiency: "The 5-Minute Photo Register (Tropy to CSV)". * Visual Phasing: "Visualising Site Phasing in Obsidian Canvas". * Literature Mining: "Using ResearchRabbit to find Irish Grey Literature".

docs.title: 2. Standardised AMS Template Library
docs.text: Development of downloadable configuration files to ensure company-wide consistency: * Zotero CSL Styles: Custom citation styles matching the AMS House Style for reports. * Tropy Metadata Profiles: Pre-configured Dublin Core templates for Irish/UK archaeology. * Obsidian Vault Starters: A "Site Starter" vault with pre-built Dataview queries for context and finds tracking.

docs.title: 3. Internal 'Digital Scholar' Accreditation
docs.text: A three-tier recognition system to gamify adoption: * DS Practitioner: Basic setup (Zotero, browser extensions, AMS email linked). * DS Specialist: Demonstrated use of synthesis tools (e.g., shared NotebookLM on a live project). * DS Fellow: Contributing new tutorials or templates to the DS Resource Site.

docs.title: 4. Specialised AMS AI Agents
docs.text: Development of internal agents trained on AMS SOPs and regional legislative requirements: * EIAR Synthesis Agent: Designed to scan TII reports for environmental mitigation trends. * CRAV Preflight Agent: Automated consistency checks for bibliographies and site codes.

docs.title: 5. Field-to-Scholar Mobile Integration
docs.text: Guidance for bridging the gap between site excavation and digital research: * Hypothesis Mobile: Protocols for site-based digital annotation of planning documents. * 3D Finds Cataloguing: Integrating Polycam/Lidar scans of finds directly into Obsidian site notes.

docs.title: 6. The 'Scholar-Consultant' Support Fund
docs.text:
Dedication of "Scholarship Hours" (e.g., 2 hours per month) for staff to use DS tools for converting grey literature into academic publications or public-facing "StoryMaps," enhancing both individual professional profiles and company reputation.

Status: Pending Strategic Review (April 2026)

docs.title: Digital Scholarship as a Catalyst for Commercial Archaeology Promotion
docs.text:
While the primary function of the AMS Digital Scholar (DS) programme is internal training and workflow optimisation, the methodologies and tools we employ offer a powerful mechanism for outwardly promoting AMS's expertise to the wider academic and commercial archaeology sectors. By shifting from a closed, service-provider model to an open, digital-first approach, we can establish AMS as a pioneer in archaeological data science.

This paper outlines strategic avenues for leveraging digital scholarship to build institutional reputation and elevate the academic profiles of individual AMS experts.

docs.title: 1. Interoperable Data & "Golden" Archives
docs.text:
The academic world relies increasingly on clean, discoverable, and reusable data. By standardising our outputs beyond the traditional "grey literature" PDF, AMS can become a vital node in the academic research network.

  • Zotero & CSL-JSON: By curating highly structured, open-access bibliographies for major infrastructure projects or regional studies (e.g., the Shannon estuary), AMS provides immediate value to academic researchers. When our datasets are easier to use and cite, our reputation for rigour is directly amplified.
  • Tropy & Dublin Core: Applying rigorous metadata standards to our site photography ensures our visual archives are interoperable with national and international repositories, demonstrating our commitment to long-term preservation standards.

docs.title: 2. Open-Source Methodologies & Tooling
docs.text:
Commercial archaeology rarely shares its internal workflows, often viewing them as proprietary advantages. However, the software engineering world has proven that open-sourcing non-sensitive tooling builds immense industry capital.

  • Sharing Obsidian Workflows: By publishing our bespoke Dataview templates for automated site registers or our Python integrations for Zotero RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), we position AMS as a technical pioneer.
  • Methodological Papers: Publishing peer-reviewed or industry white papers detailing how we built these workflows establishes our consultants as thought leaders in archaeological informatics.

docs.title: 3. Public Annotation & Thought Leadership
docs.text:
While AMS currently utilises Hypothesis for private, confidential reviews of planning documents or EIARs, the platform's public layer presents a unique opportunity for engagement.

  • Active Commentary: AMS experts can use Hypothesis to publicly annotate new national guidelines (e.g., TII standards), major academic papers, or policy documents. This public "layer" of expert commentary demonstrates active engagement with the discipline's cutting edge and inserts AMS directly into the academic and policy conversation.

docs.title: 4. Interactive Heritage & Spatial Storytelling
docs.text:
Digital scholarship moves beyond flat text. The integration of our Obsidian Knowledge Graphs with spatial data derived from our BIM strategy (e.g., LiDAR scans, photogrammetry, or HBIM models) allows for rich, interactive outputs.

  • StoryMaps & Digital Twins: Publishing interactive digital models or "StoryMaps" of major excavations provides a highly engaging, visual demonstration of our expertise. These are highly effective for public outreach, client presentations, and academic conferences, moving beyond the traditional PowerPoint format.

docs.title: 5. Algorithmic Transparency and Ethical AI
docs.text:
As AI becomes more prevalent in research, demonstrating algorithmic transparency builds immense trust.

  • The CRAV Protocol: By publicly detailing how we use tools like Research Rabbit or Perplexity—and critically, how we verify their outputs via the Check, Review, Approve, Verify (CRAV) protocol—we demonstrate responsible, ethical adoption of advanced technology. This mitigates the "black box" stigma often associated with AI in heritage management.

docs.title: Building the Profile of Individual Experts
docs.text: The institutional reputation of AMS is inextricably linked to the standing of its individual consultants and researchers. Digital scholarship provides the tools to cultivate these individual academic profiles without requiring a return to full-time academia.

docs.title: The "Consultant-Scholar" Model
docs.text:
The traditional divide between "academic" and "commercial" archaeology is narrowing. We can support our staff in becoming "Consultant-Scholars" through the following initiatives:

  1. ORCID Integration: Mandating and supporting the creation of ORCID iDs for all senior staff. Every public report, dataset, or methodology paper produced by AMS should be linked to the author's ORCID profile, building a persistent, verifiable academic record.
  2. Micro-Publishing: Encouraging staff to publish short, targeted insights or code snippets (e.g., a novel spatial analysis script or a unique chronological observation from a site) on the AMS technical blog or via academic pre-print servers, rather than waiting years for a final monograph.
  3. Digital Portfolios (Obsidian Publish): Supporting key experts in maintaining public-facing digital portfolios or curated sub-sets of their Obsidian Knowledge Graphs. This allows them to showcase their specific areas of expertise (e.g., medieval urbanism, archaeometallurgy) to the wider community.
  4. Academic Networking (Research Rabbit): Training staff to use tools like Research Rabbit not just for literature reviews, but to identify and connect with academic peers working on similar problems, fostering collaborative research opportunities and joint funding applications.

By investing in the digital profiles of our team members, AMS ensures that our collective expertise is visible, citable, and recognised at the highest levels of the profession.

docs.title: AI Discovery: Perplexity & Research Rabbit
docs.text: Artificial Intelligence discovery tools are revolutionising how we map the research landscape for archaeological consultancy. For the AMS Digital Scholar (DS) programme, we utilise Perplexity for rapid synthesis and Research Rabbit for visualising citation networks.

docs.title: Perplexity: The Research Engine
docs.text: Perplexity is an AI-powered search engine that provides direct answers to complex questions, backed by real-world citations. It is available at perplexity.ai and is used at AMS for: * Legislative Summaries: "What are the current requirements for underwater archaeology under the Irish National Monuments Act?" * Regional Context: "Summarise the Mesolithic archaeology of the Shannon estuary based on recent TII reports." * Rapid Fact-Checking: Verifying site names, dates, and historical figures during the drafting process.

docs.title: Best Practices for Perplexity
docs.text:
• Verify Sources: Always click the citations to ensure the AI hasn't "hallucinated" or misinterpreted a source.
  • Use "Pro" Mode: For complex archaeological queries, use the 'Pro' or 'Writing' modes for deeper analysis.
  • UK/Ireland Focus: Explicitly ask for results focused on UK and Irish standards to avoid US-centric legal drift.

docs.title: Research Rabbit: Mapping the Network
docs.text: Research Rabbit is a "Spotify for Papers" that allows you to visually map how academic papers and reports are connected.

docs.title: Key Workflows
docs.text:
• Seed Papers: Add a key publication (e.g., a foundational paper on Irish fulachtaí fia) to a collection.
  • Visualise: Research Rabbit will show you a "Map" of every paper that has cited that source, and every source that paper cited.
  • Discover: It suggests "Similar Work" and "Early/Later Work," helping you find obscure but relevant reports that might have been missed in a standard keyword search.

docs.title: Integration with the AMS Ecosystem
docs.text:
The primary goal of discovery tools is to populate our permanent reference archive.

  • Zotero Sync: Both Perplexity and Research Rabbit allow for easy export to Zotero. Once you discover a relevant source in Research Rabbit, you can save it to your Zotero Group Library with one click.
    • YouTube: ResearchRabbit & Zotero Sync Tutorial
  • Workflow Integration: Use Research Rabbit to find foundation papers and then use Perplexity to find real-time, grey-literature reports that have not yet been indexed in major academic databases.

docs.title: Google NotebookLM: The Synthesis Engine
docs.text:
The potential for Google NotebookLM to bridge the gap between discovery (Perplexity/Research Rabbit) and archival (Zotero) is a critical part of the Digital Scholar workflow.

  • Perplexity Integration: Using third-party extensions, researchers can perform one-click exports of complex Perplexity discovery conversations directly into a grounded notebook for synthesis. This preserves all discovered source links and citations, ensuring the synthesis is verifiable and traceable.
  • Zotero Integration: By syncing Zotero PDF storage to a tracked Google Drive folder, NotebookLM can "watch" and automatically index new archaeological reports as they are added to the library, providing real-time AI reasoning across the entire project archive.

For a deep dive into this workflow, see the Google NotebookLM tool page.

docs.title: Access for AMS Staff
docs.text:
• Perplexity: Access via the shared AMS corporate login (contact the AI Team Lead for details).
  • Research Rabbit: Sign up for a free account at researchrabbit.ai using your AMS email.

Warning: AI tools are for discovery and synthesis. They must NEVER be used to write final report text without rigorous human review and verification via the CRAV protocol.

docs.title: Hypothesis: Collaborative Evidence Annotation
docs.text: Hypothesis is a web-based tool that allows the AMS team to collaboratively annotate PDFs and web pages in real-time. It is the primary tool for the "Peer-Review" phase of our digital scholarship, enabling consultants to share insights directly on the source material.

docs.title: Why Hypothesis for AMS?
docs.text:
• Real-Time Collaboration: Multiple consultants can highlight and comment on the same planning document or EIAR simultaneously.
  • Public & Private Groups: We use Private AMS Groups to ensure client confidentiality while still allowing for internal knowledge sharing.
  • Traceable Insights: Every highlight is attributed to a specific staff member, creating an audit trail of the research process.

docs.title: 1. Reviewing Planning Conditions
docs.text: When a new project is launched, the Project Lead can share a link to the Planning Conditions. Team members can highlight critical requirements and tag them (e.g., #Mitigation, #Geophysics, #Testing).

docs.title: 2. Peer-Review of Grey Literature
docs.text: When reading a site report from a previous excavation, consultants can use Hypothesis to flag inconsistencies or notable finds that may impact our current project.

docs.title: 3. Exporting Evidence
docs.text: Annotations can be exported to Markdown and imported into Obsidian. This ensures that the insights gained during the reading phase are directly integrated into the writing phase.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use Tags: Always tag your annotations with the relevant Site ID or Subject Matter.
  • Be Professional: Remember that annotations in a Private Group are visible to all AMS team members. Use clear, formal language.
  • Stick to Private Groups: Ensure you are logged into the AMS Internal Research Group before annotating sensitive client documents.

docs.title: Setup Guide for AMS Staff
docs.text:
1. Sign Up: Create an account at web.hypothes.is using your AMS email.
  2. Extension: Install the Hypothesis browser extension for Chrome or Edge.
  3. Groups: Join the AMS Internal Research group using the link provided in the AI Strategy resource site.
  4. Annotate: Click the Hypothesis icon in your browser to start highlighting.

For a guide on exporting annotations to Obsidian, see our Tutorials.

docs.title: Google NotebookLM: The Cognitive Operating System
docs.text: Google NotebookLM is a foundational tool for the AMS Digital Scholar (DS) programme, serving as a "Cognitive Operating System" for complex archaeological research. It allows staff to upload a curated collection of sources—PDFs, website URLs, and YouTube transcripts—and use a grounded AI to synthesise, query, and transform that data into actionable insights.

docs.title: Why NotebookLM for AMS?
docs.text:
• Source Grounding: Unlike general AI models, NotebookLM is strictly "grounded" in your uploaded sources. It will not cite information outside of your project files, virtually eliminating the risk of AI hallucinations.
  • Multimedia Synthesis: It can transform dense site reports into Audio Overviews (AI podcasts) or Video Presentations, making it an ideal tool for rapid internal briefings or client previews.
  • Massive Context: With a 1-million-token context window per source and support for up to 300 sources, it can ingest the entire "grey literature" history of a major landscape project in seconds.

docs.title: 1. Integration with Perplexity (Discovery to Synthesis)
docs.text: AMS researchers use Perplexity to discover the latest web-based data and official site reports. Using the Perplexity to NotebookLM extension, these findings are exported directly into a focused notebook. This creates a seamless pipeline from real-time web search to deep, grounded analysis, bypassing the need for manual copy-pasting and ensuring every synthesis is backed by a verified URL.

docs.title: 2. Integration with Zotero (Evidence to Archive)
docs.text:
While NotebookLM handles the active synthesis, Zotero remains our primary archive.

  • PDF Sync: By syncing your Zotero PDF storage to a Google Drive folder, NotebookLM can "watch" your library and automatically update its knowledge base as you add new sources. This ensures the AI is always querying the most recent version of your project literature.
  • Insight Export: Use the NotebookLM to Zotero extension to move AI-generated Q&As, summaries, and key citations back into your permanent Zotero project library for long-term reference and citation in final reports.

docs.title: 3. Collaborative Review
docs.text: Project Leads can share a "Notebook" with their team. This allows multiple consultants to query the same set of evidence (e.g., "What are the common stratigraphic themes across all five test-trenching reports?") and share "Saved Notes" of key AI insights.

docs.title: Video Tutorials & Workflow Guides
docs.text:
For visual guidance on mastering the NotebookLM integration, see these recommended tutorials:

  • The Ultimate Research Workflow (Perplexity & NotebookLM): A deep dive into using Perplexity for discovery and NotebookLM for grounded synthesis.
    • YouTube: Perplexity + NotebookLM Tutorial
  • Zotero & NotebookLM Workflow: Practical steps for moving your Zotero-managed PDFs into the NotebookLM environment.
    • YouTube: Zotero & NotebookLM Guide
  • Audio Overviews & Interactive Features: How to generate and interact with AI podcasts based on your research data.
    • YouTube: NotebookLM Audio Overviews Tutorial

docs.title: Key Features for 2026
docs.text:
• Interactive Audio: Join the "hosts" of your Audio Overview to ask real-time questions during the AI-generated briefing.
  • Studio Assets: Generate mind maps, infographics, and stratigraphic tables directly from your project notes with one click.
  • Gemini Sync: Access and query your notebooks directly from the main Gemini interface for mobile field use.

docs.title: Setup Guide for AMS Staff
docs.text:
1. Access: Log in to notebooklm.google.com using your AMS corporate account.
  2. Create: Start a new notebook named after your Site ID or Project Name.
  3. Sources: Upload relevant EIARs, NMS records, or TII reports.
  4. Extensions: Ensure the Perplexity to NotebookLM and NotebookLM to Zotero extensions are active in your browser.

For a detailed tutorial on the search-to-synthesis pipeline, see our AI Discovery Guide.

docs.title: Obsidian: Knowledge Management & Networked Thought
docs.text: Obsidian is the primary "Knowledge Graph" tool for the AMS Digital Scholar (DS) programme. It is a powerful Markdown-based application that allows researchers to link notes, creating a "Second Brain" for complex archaeological projects. For AMS, it bridges the gap between raw site data and the final narrative in our reports.

docs.title: Why Obsidian for AMS?
docs.text:
• Non-Linear Research: Archaeology is rarely linear. Obsidian allows us to link a Site ID to a Period, a Find Type, or a Historical Figure using [[Wikilinks]].
  • Local & Secure: Unlike cloud-based tools, Obsidian stores files locally on AMS servers as plain Markdown (.md). This ensures long-term data preservation and client confidentiality.
  • Automated Registers: Using the Dataview plugin, we can automatically generate lists of contexts, finds, or stratigraphic units directly from our field notes.

docs.title: 1. The "Second Brain" for Sites
docs.text: Create a master note for every major excavation or consultancy project. Use links to connect the site to: * [[Relevant Legislation]] (e.g., National Monuments Acts). * [[Geographical Context]] (Townlands, Counties, River catchments). * [[Comparative Sites]] (Earlier excavations in the same region).

docs.title: 2. Strategic Narrative Development
docs.text: Use Obsidian to draft the "Discussion" sections of Desk-Based Assessments (DBAs). By linking disparate pieces of evidence (e.g., a specific lithic scatter linked to a post-glacial climate event), the AI can help synthesise these connections into a professional narrative.

docs.title: 3. Zotero Integration
docs.text: Use the Zotero Integration plugin to import your citations and annotations directly into Obsidian. This creates a searchable database of every paper or report the AMS team has ever read.

docs.title: Recommended Plugins for AMS
docs.text:
• Dataview: To create dynamic tables and lists of site data.
  • Templater: To ensure every site note follows the AMS standard structure.
  • Canvas: For visual brainstorming and mapping out stratigraphic relationships or site phasing.

docs.title: Setup Guide for AMS Staff
docs.text:
1. Download: Install Obsidian from obsidian.md.
  2. Vault: Create a new "Vault" on your project-specific OneDrive or server folder.
  3. Core Settings: Enable "Files & Links" -> "Automatically update internal links."
  4. Community Plugins: Browse and install Dataview and Zotero Integration.

For a tutorial on building your first archaeological vault, see the Tutorials section.

docs.title: Tropy: Managing Archaeological Imagery
docs.text: Tropy is an open-source tool designed specifically for researchers to organise and describe large collections of digital photos. For AMS, Tropy is the essential link between raw field photography (site photos, sections, finds) and the structured metadata required for professional archive deposition.

docs.title: Why Tropy for AMS?
docs.text:
• Standardised Metadata: Tropy allows us to attach Dublin Core or custom archaeological metadata to every photo (e.g., Site Code, Context Number, Direction of View).
  • Bulk Editing: Quickly update metadata for hundreds of site photos at once, saving hours of manual data entry.
  • Transcription & Notes: Add detailed transcriptions of site notebooks or field sketches directly to the associated image.

docs.title: 1. Custom Metadata Templates
docs.text: AMS staff should use the 'AMS Archaeology Template' in Tropy. This includes fields for: * Site Code: The unique project identifier. * Context/Feature: The specific stratigraphic unit. * Subject: (e.g., Section, Plan, Post-excavation find). * Photographer: To ensure proper attribution in final reports.

docs.title: 2. Photo Organisation
docs.text: Tropy does not move your files; it creates a database that points to them. You can group photos into 'Items' (e.g., all photos of a single burial) and 'Lists' (e.g., all photos from Week 1 of an excavation).

docs.title: 3. Export for Reporting
docs.text: Once your photos are described, you can export the metadata as a CSV or JSON file. This can be used to automatically generate the "Photo Register" appendix in your final report.

docs.title: Integration with the AMS Ecosystem
docs.text:
• Obsidian: Link to specific Tropy items or exported images from your site notes.
  • Final Reports: Use exported CSV data to populate the photo tables in Word using the AMS Document Factory.

docs.title: Setup Guide for AMS Staff
docs.text:
1. Download: Install Tropy from tropy.org.
  2. Project: Create a new Tropy project for your current site.
  3. Template: Go to Settings -> Templates and import the AMS Metadata Standard.
  4. Import: Drag and drop your site photos to begin describing them.

For the AMS Metadata Standard file, please check the Research folder.

docs.title: Zotero: Reference Management for Digital Scholarship
docs.text: Zotero is the primary reference management solution for the AMS Digital Scholar (DS) programme. It is an open-source, community-driven tool designed to collect, organise, cite, and share research sources. For AMS, it serves as a centralised "Digital Library" for managing both academic journals and the high volume of grey literature (site reports, EIARs, and client briefings) characteristic of our industry.

docs.title: Why Zotero for AMS?
docs.text:
• Grey Literature Management: Unlike other tools, Zotero excels at handling unpublished archaeological reports, allowing for manual metadata entry (Site Codes, Townlands, and County data).
  • Collaborative Power: Group Libraries enable teams to sync references and annotated PDFs across multiple users and devices, ensuring everyone on a project is using the same source of truth.
  • Seamless Integration: Works directly with Microsoft Word (for formal reports), Google Docs (for collaborative drafting), and modern digital tools like Obsidian and MkDocs.

docs.title: 1. Group Libraries
docs.text: AMS project teams can create Private Group Libraries. These are shared spaces where all members can see the same collection of papers, notes, and PDF files. * Action: Project Leads should create the group and invite team members as 'Admins' or 'Members'.

docs.title: 2. Collaborative PDF Annotation
docs.text: Since Zotero 6, the built-in PDF reader allows for team-based highlighting and commenting. * Note: Annotations are synced to the group database, identifying which team member made a specific observation. This is ideal for peer-reviewing archaeological assessments.

docs.title: 3. The "Inbox" Workflow
docs.text: To maintain a high-quality library, AMS recommends the Inbox method: * New sources are dropped into an _INBOX collection. * The Project Lead or a designated 'Librarian' reviews the metadata (ensuring the author, year, and site title are correct) before moving the item to the permanent project folder.

docs.title: Best Practices for Archaeological Data
docs.text:
• Standardised Tagging: Use a unified tagging system for Site IDs, Periods (e.g., Mesolithic, Medieval), and Material Types (Lithics, Ceramics).
  • CRAV Protocol: Always apply the Check, Review, Approve, Verify protocol to imported metadata. Automated imports from web browsers often miss Site Codes or specific Irish/UK townland spellings.
  • Company Ownership: Group Libraries should be 'owned' by a generic AMS Research account (e.g., ai@ams-archaeology.com) rather than an individual staff member, ensuring continuity if personnel changes.

docs.title: Better BibTeX (BBT)
docs.text: For technical reporting using Markdown or LaTeX, the Better BibTeX plugin is essential. It generates stable citation keys (e.g., Brayne2024SiteX) that remain consistent across the entire team.

docs.title: Zotero Connector
docs.text: Install the browser extension to save reports directly from national heritage databases like the National Monuments Service (NMS) or the Heritage Gateway.

docs.title: Tutorials & Integration Guides
docs.text:
To master the Zotero ecosystem within the AMS workflow, we recommend the following resources:

  • ResearchRabbit & Zotero Sync: Learn how to connect your Zotero library to ResearchRabbit for automated literature mapping.
    • YouTube: ResearchRabbit & Zotero Sync (Bryan Jenks)
  • Zotero 7 Overview: A comprehensive guide to the latest features, including the built-in PDF reader and annotation tools.
    • YouTube: Zotero 7 Full Tutorial

docs.title: Setup Guide for AMS Staff
docs.text:
1. Download: Install Zotero from zotero.org.
  2. Account: Register using your AMS email address.
  3. Groups: Check your email for invitations to AMS Project Groups.
  4. Browser: Install the Zotero Connector for Chrome or Edge.

For further assistance or to request a new Group Library, please contact the AI Strategy team.

docs.title: AMS Digital Scholar: Tutorials
docs.text: Welcome to the Digital Scholar (DS) tutorial library. These step-by-step guides are designed to help AMS staff master the tools of digital scholarship.

docs.title: Available Tutorials
docs.text:
• Setting up your first Zotero Group Library
  • Visualising Research Networks with Research Rabbit
  • AI-Powered Discovery: Perplexity & Research Rabbit
  • Building an Archaeological Knowledge Graph in Obsidian
  • Collaborative Annotation with Hypothesis
  • Managing Archaeological Imagery with Tropy

If you have a request for a specific tutorial, please contact the AI Strategy team.

docs.title: AI-Powered Discovery: Perplexity & Research Rabbit
docs.text: This tutorial explores how to use AI tools to rapidly map the archaeological research landscape. We focus on Perplexity for synthesis and Research Rabbit for citation mapping.

docs.title: 1. Perplexity: The Research Engine
docs.text: Perplexity provides direct answers with citations. It is excellent for legislative summaries and regional context.

docs.title: Workflow:
docs.text:
1. Ask: "What are the archaeological requirements for peatland development in Ireland?"
  2. Refine: Use the "Pro" mode for a deeper dive into recent planning precedents.
  3. Verify: Always click the citations to confirm the source material before including it in a report.

docs.title: 2. Research Rabbit: Mapping Citations
docs.text: Research Rabbit allows you to find "missing" papers by visualising how publications are linked.

docs.title: Workflow:
docs.text:
1. Seed: Add 1-2 key papers on your topic (e.g., a specific period or site type).
  2. Discover: Click "Similar Work" to see a visual map of related publications.
  3. Export: Select relevant papers and export them to your Zotero Group Library.

docs.title: Research Rabbit: Getting Started
docs.text: Note: AI tools are for discovery. All findings must be verified via the CRAV protocol.

docs.title: Collaborative Annotation with Hypothesis
docs.text: Hypothesis allows the AMS team to collaboratively annotate PDFs and web pages in real-time. This guide covers setting up your account and participating in private AMS research groups.

docs.title: 1. Getting Started
docs.text:
1. Sign Up: Create an account at web.hypothes.is using your AMS email.
  2. Install Extension: Add the Hypothesis extension to your browser (Chrome, Edge, or Firefox).
  3. Log In: Click the Hypothesis icon in your browser toolbar and log in.

docs.title: 2. Joining the AMS Private Group
docs.text: To ensure client confidentiality, all project-related annotations MUST occur within private groups. 1. Request the AMS Internal Research Group invite link from the AI Team Lead. 2. Once joined, ensure you select the group from the dropdown menu in the Hypothesis sidebar before you start annotating.

docs.title: 3. Annotating a Document
docs.text:
• Highlight: Select text on a webpage or PDF to highlight it.
  • Annotate: Select text and click the "Annotate" icon to add a comment.
  • Tags: Use tags like #Mitigation, #Geophysics, or the Site ID to make annotations searchable.

docs.title: 4. Best Practices for AMS Staff
docs.text:
• Professionalism: Annotations are visible to the entire team. Use formal, professional language.
  • Privacy: Never annotate sensitive client documents in the "Public" layer.
  • Linguistic Standard: Use Standard English (UK & Ireland) in all comments.

docs.title: 5. Official Video Tutorial
docs.text:
Watch this "Hypothesis 101" video to see social annotation in action.

For more information on exporting these insights, see the Obsidian Tutorial.

docs.title: Building an Archaeological Knowledge Graph in Obsidian
docs.text: This tutorial guides AMS staff through setting up a "Knowledge Graph" for archaeological research using Obsidian. By the end of this guide, you will have a structured vault that links sites, periods, and legislation.

docs.title: 1. Why use Obsidian?
docs.text: Archaeology is non-linear. Obsidian allows you to connect disparate pieces of evidence (e.g., a specific lithic scatter linked to a post-glacial climate event) using [[Wikilinks]]. This creates a searchable, networked database of your research.

docs.title: 2. Setting Up Your Vault
docs.text:
1. Download & Install: Get Obsidian from obsidian.md.
  2. Create a Vault: Choose a folder on your project-specific OneDrive or AMS server. Name it "AMS_Digital_Scholar_Vault".
  3. Core Settings:
    • Go to Settings -> Files & Links.
    • Enable "Automatically update internal links".
    • Set "Default location for new attachments" to a specific folder (e.g., _attachments).

docs.title: 3. Creating Your First Site Note
docs.text:
Create a new note named after your Site ID (e.g., A056_Tara_Meath). Use the following structure:

# Site: A056 - Tara, Meath

## Metadata
*   **Site Code:** A056
*   **Period:** [[Iron Age]], [[Medieval]]
*   **County:** [[Meath]]
*   **Legislation:** [[National Monuments Act 1930]]

## Summary
Brief description of the site and findings.

## Related Research
*   Linked to [[Comparative_Site_B]]
*   See annotations in [[Zotero_Notes_A056]]

docs.title: 4. Visualising the Graph
docs.text: Click the Graph View icon on the left sidebar. As you add more notes and links, you will see a visual representation of how your research is connected.

docs.title: 5. Official Video Tutorial
docs.text:
For a foundational overview of the Obsidian interface and core features, watch this official talk from the Obsidian team.

Next Step: Learn how to integrate Zotero with Obsidian.

docs.title: Tutorial: Visualising Research Networks with Research Rabbit
docs.text: Research Rabbit is a "Spotify for Papers" that revolutionises how the AMS team maps the research landscape for archaeological consultancy. This tutorial guides you through using it to discover connected site reports, academic papers, and grey literature.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A registered Research Rabbit account (using your @ams-archaeology.com email).
  • A Zotero account (highly recommended for seamless syncing).

docs.title: Step 1: Start with a "Seed" Paper
docs.text: The most effective way to use Research Rabbit is to start with a "Seed" paper—a foundational source for your project. 1. Log in to researchrabbit.ai. 2. Click "Add Papers". 3. Search for a key publication (e.g., a major TII project report or a seminal paper on your site type). 4. Add it to a new collection (e.g., AMS - [Site Code]).

docs.title: Step 2: Visualise the Network
docs.text: Once you have added a seed paper, Research Rabbit will generate a visual map: * Similar Work: Shows papers with overlapping themes and citations. * Early Work: Displays the older, foundational research that your seed paper cited. * Later Work: Lists more recent publications that have cited your seed paper since it was published.

docs.title: Step 3: Interactive Discovery
docs.text:
• Click Nodes: Click on any paper in the map to see its abstract, authors, and citation count.
  • Explore Authors: Click an author's name to see their entire publication network and find other relevant experts in the field.
  • The "Rabbit Hole": Add any interesting papers you find back into your collection. The map will dynamically update to find more papers similar to your new additions.

docs.title: Step 4: Sync with Zotero
docs.text: Research Rabbit integrates directly with Zotero: 1. Go to your Research Rabbit settings and link your Zotero account. 2. Once linked, you can sync your Research Rabbit collections directly to a Zotero Group Library. 3. This ensures that any new sources discovered by the AI are immediately available to the entire AMS project team.

docs.title: Video Guide: Getting Started with Research Rabbit
docs.text:
For a visual walkthrough of these steps, please watch this excellent overview:

🔗 Mastering Research Rabbit for Literature Mapping

docs.title: Best Practices for AMS
docs.text:
• Use Project Codes: Name your collections using the AMS Site Code for easy identification.
  • Collaborate: Share your collections with other AMS team members to build a unified research landscape.
  • Verify via CRAV: AI-discovered papers are high-signal leads, but always perform a Check, Review, Approve, Verify check before citing them in a formal report.

For more information on the role of AI in discovery, see our AI Tools Page.

docs.title: Managing Archaeological Imagery with Tropy
docs.text: Tropy is the essential tool for organising and describing large collections of digital photos. This tutorial explains how to apply the AMS Metadata Standard to your site photography.

docs.title: 1. Installation & Project Setup
docs.text:
1. Download: Install Tropy from tropy.org.
  2. New Project: Open Tropy and select File -> New Project. Save it as SiteCode_Photography_Project.
  3. Importing Photos: Drag and drop your site photos directly into the Tropy window.

docs.title: 2. Applying the AMS Metadata Standard
docs.text: AMS uses a specific metadata schema to ensure compatibility with national archives. 1. Go to Settings -> Templates. 2. Import the AMS_Archaeology_Template.ttp (available in the research/ folder). 3. Select an image and apply the template from the metadata pane on the right.

docs.title: 3. Bulk Editing
docs.text: To save time, you can apply metadata to multiple photos at once: 1. Select multiple photos in the item view. 2. Update a field (e.g., Site Code or Photographer) in the metadata pane. 3. The change will be applied to all selected items.

docs.title: 4. Exporting for Reports
docs.text: Once your photos are described, you can export the data for use in the AMS Document Factory: 1. Select the items you wish to export. 2. Go to File -> Export. 3. Choose CSV to generate a photo register that can be inserted into your Word report.

docs.title: 5. Official Video Tutorial
docs.text:
This "Getting Started" video from the Tropy team covers the basics of photo management and metadata.

Learn more about metadata standards in the Tropy Tool Review.

docs.title: Tutorial: Setting up an AMS Zotero Group Library
docs.text: This tutorial guides AMS Project Leads through the process of creating and managing a Zotero Group Library. Group Libraries are the cornerstone of the Digital Scholar (DS) programme, enabling real-time collaboration on site reports, academic papers, and grey literature.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A registered Zotero account (using your @ams-archaeology.com email).
  • Zotero Desktop installed on your machine.
  • Zotero Connector installed in your browser.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Group
docs.text:
1. Log in to zotero.org in your browser.
  2. Navigate to the Groups tab in the top header.
  3. Click "Create a New Group".
  4. Group Name: Use the standard AMS format: AMS - [Project Name/Site Code] (e.g., AMS - Kildare-Meath Upgrade).
  5. Group Type: Select Private Membership. This ensures that only invited AMS staff can see the library and its contents.

docs.title: Step 2: Configure Library Settings
docs.text: Once the group is created, set the following 'Library Settings' to ensure maximum collaboration: * Library Reading: Any group member. * Library Editing: Any group member. * File Editing: Any group member. * Action: Click "Save Settings".

docs.title: Step 3: Invite the Team
docs.text:
1. Go to Member Settings within your new group.
  2. Click "Send More Invitations".
  3. Enter the AMS email addresses of your project team.
  4. Important: Also invite the generic company account ai@ams-archaeology.com and set it to 'Admin' status. This ensures the library remains accessible if an individual staff member leaves.

docs.title: Step 4: Sync to Desktop
docs.text:
1. Open your Zotero Desktop application.
  2. Click the green 'Sync' icon in the top right corner.
  3. Your new Group Library will now appear in the left-hand pane under "Group Libraries".

docs.title: Step 5: Establishing the "Inbox" Workflow
docs.text: To keep the library professional and clean, create the following collection structure: 1. Right-click on your Group Library and select "New Collection". 2. Name it _INBOX. 3. Instruct your team to drop all new web-clipped sources into this folder first. 4. The Project Lead will then verify the metadata (following the CRAV protocol) before moving the item to the permanent project folders (e.g., Planning Documents, Comparative Sites, Specialist Reports).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Files not syncing? Ensure you have accepted the invitation in your email before attempting to sync.
  • Metadata is messy? Use the "Right-click -> Retrieve Metadata for PDF" feature, but always perform a manual check for Site Codes and Townland names.

For more advanced tips, including ZotFile and Better BibTeX, see the Zotero Tool Page.
